chapter: Ch 3 — Theory of Production and Cost

questions.stem: The reward earned by land as a factor of production is called:

options.text: rent
options.explanation: Correct. Land is the free gift of nature used in production, and its reward is rent.

options.text: wages
options.explanation: Wages are the reward of labour, not land.

options.text: interest
options.explanation: Interest is the reward of capital, not land.

options.text: profit
options.explanation: Profit is the reward of the entrepreneur, not land.

questions.sourceRef: Factor rewards: land → rent, labour → wages, capital → interest, entrepreneur → profit

questions.stem: Capital as a factor of production is best described as:

options.text: the free gifts of nature used in production
options.explanation: That describes land, not capital.

options.text: the man-made produced means of production, whose reward is interest
options.explanation: Correct. Capital is itself the result of past production — machines, tools, buildings, stock — and its reward is interest.

options.text: every human effort directed at production, whose reward is wages
options.explanation: That describes labour, not capital.

options.text: the person who bears the risk of the venture
options.explanation: That describes the entrepreneur, not capital.

questions.sourceRef: Capital = produced (man-made) means of production; reward is interest

questions.stem: Which factor of production bears the uncertainty and risk of the business and earns the residual reward?

options.text: Land
options.explanation: Land earns rent, a contractual reward, and does not bear the venture's risk.

options.text: Labour
options.explanation: Labour earns wages, a contractual reward, and does not bear the residual risk.

options.text: Capital
options.explanation: Capital earns interest, a contractual reward, and does not bear the residual risk.

options.text: Entrepreneur
options.explanation: Correct. The entrepreneur organises the other factors, bears risk and uncertainty, and takes profit — the residual, the only reward that can be negative.

questions.sourceRef: Entrepreneur bears risk and receives the residual reward, profit

questions.stem: The production function expresses the relationship between:

options.text: the prices of inputs and the price of output
options.explanation: That is a cost or revenue relationship. The production function is a physical, not a price, relationship.

options.text: the physical inputs used and the maximum output obtainable from them
options.explanation: Correct. Q = f(L, K) states the maximum output a firm can produce from given quantities of inputs, at the given technology.

options.text: total revenue and total cost
options.explanation: That is the profit relationship, not the production function.

options.text: quantity demanded and price
options.explanation: That is the demand function, not the production function.

questions.sourceRef: Production function Q = f(L, K): maximum output from given inputs

questions.stem: In the theory of production, the short run is a period in which:

options.text: at least one factor of production is fixed
options.explanation: Correct. The short run is defined by at least one fixed factor (usually the plant), so output is varied only by changing the variable factors.

options.text: all factors of production can be varied
options.explanation: That is the long run, in which no factor is fixed.

options.text: it lasts exactly three months
options.explanation: The short run is not defined by clock time; it is defined by having at least one fixed factor.

options.text: output cannot be changed at all
options.explanation: Output can be changed in the short run by varying the variable factors on the fixed plant.

readLink.label: Read: Short run and long run, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: Short run: at least one factor fixed

questions.stem: The long run in production theory is best defined as the period in which:

options.text: the firm has been operating for more than one year
options.explanation: The long run is not a fixed clock length; a year may be short or long run depending on the industry.

options.text: only labour can be varied
options.explanation: Varying only labour against a fixed plant is the short run, not the long run.

options.text: all factors of production, including plant and capital, can be varied
options.explanation: Correct. In the long run every factor is variable — the firm can change its plant and all inputs — so there is no fixed factor.

options.text: the state of technology can never change
options.explanation: The long-run definition concerns the variability of factors, not a frozen technology.

readLink.label: Read: Short run and long run, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: Long run: all factors variable, no fixed factor

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Production · Law of variable proportions
questions.stem: The law of variable proportions applies to a situation in which:

options.text: all factors are increased in the same proportion
options.explanation: That is returns to scale (a long-run idea), not the law of variable proportions.

options.text: more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor in the short run
options.explanation: Correct. The law of variable proportions (returns to a factor) studies the short run, where a variable factor is added to a fixed factor and the proportions between them change.

options.text: the firm builds a larger plant
options.explanation: Building a larger plant is a long-run change; the law of variable proportions is a short-run law with a fixed factor.

options.text: all factors are fixed
options.explanation: If all factors were fixed, output could not vary at all; the law requires one variable and one fixed factor.

readLink.label: Read: The law of variable proportions, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: Law of variable proportions: variable factor added to a fixed factor (short run)

questions.stem: A fixed plot yields a total product of 24 units with 2 workers and 39 units with 3 workers. The marginal product of the 3rd worker is:

options.text: 39 units
options.explanation: 39 is the total product with 3 workers, not the marginal product. Marginal product is the change in total product.

options.text: 15 units
options.explanation: Correct. MP of the 3rd worker = TP(3) − TP(2) = 39 − 24 = 15 units.

options.text: 13 units
options.explanation: 13 is the average product with 3 workers (39 ÷ 3), not the marginal product.

options.text: 24 units
options.explanation: 24 is the total product with 2 workers, not the marginal product of the 3rd worker.

readLink.label: Read: The law of variable proportions, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: MP = ΔTP = TP(n) − TP(n − 1)

questions.stem: The total product of a farm is 52 units when 4 workers are employed. The average product of labour is:

options.text: 52 units
options.explanation: 52 is the total product, not the average product per worker.

options.text: 48 units
options.explanation: 48 does not follow from 52 ÷ 4. Average product = total product ÷ number of workers.

options.text: 13 units
options.explanation: Correct. AP = TP ÷ L = 52 ÷ 4 = 13 units per worker.

options.text: 15 units
options.explanation: 15 is the marginal product of an earlier worker in the schedule, not the average product at 4 workers.

readLink.label: Read: The law of variable proportions, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: AP = TP ÷ L

questions.stem: Total product is 52 units with 4 workers and 60 units with 5 workers. The marginal product of the 5th worker is:

options.text: 12 units
options.explanation: 12 is the average product at 5 workers (60 ÷ 5), not the marginal product.

options.text: 8 units
options.explanation: Correct. MP of the 5th worker = TP(5) − TP(4) = 60 − 52 = 8 units.

options.text: 60 units
options.explanation: 60 is the total product with 5 workers, not the marginal product.

options.text: 4 units
options.explanation: 4 is not the difference 60 − 52; the marginal product is 8 units.

readLink.label: Read: The law of variable proportions, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: MP = ΔTP = TP(n) − TP(n − 1)

questions.stem: A firm's total product is 66 units when 6 workers are employed. The average product of labour is:

options.text: 11 units
options.explanation: Correct. AP = TP ÷ L = 66 ÷ 6 = 11 units per worker.

options.text: 66 units
options.explanation: 66 is the total product, not the average product per worker.

options.text: 60 units
options.explanation: 60 is the total product at 5 workers in the schedule, not the average product at 6 workers.

options.text: 13 units
options.explanation: 13 is the peak average product (reached earlier at 4 workers), not the average product at 6 workers.

readLink.label: Read: The law of variable proportions, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: AP = TP ÷ L

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Production · MP and AP relationship
questions.stem: Average product of a variable factor is at its maximum at the level of employment where:

options.text: marginal product is at its own maximum
options.explanation: Marginal product peaks earlier, one unit before average product; the two maxima do not coincide.

options.text: marginal product equals average product
options.explanation: Correct. Average product is highest where the marginal product has fallen to equal it; beyond that point MP is below AP and AP falls.

options.text: marginal product is zero
options.explanation: Where marginal product is zero, total product is at its maximum, not average product.

options.text: marginal product is negative
options.explanation: Negative marginal product marks Stage III, where total product falls; it is not where average product peaks.

readLink.label: Read: The law of variable proportions, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: AP is maximum where MP = AP

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Production · MP and AP relationship
questions.stem: So long as marginal product is greater than average product, the average product will:

options.text: fall
options.explanation: Average product falls only when marginal product is below it, not above it.

options.text: rise
options.explanation: Correct. When the marginal unit adds more than the running average, it pulls the average up, so average product rises.

options.text: stay constant
options.explanation: Average product is constant only at the instant MP equals AP, not while MP exceeds AP.

options.text: become negative
options.explanation: Average product cannot be negative while output is positive; the marginal-average link governs its direction, not its sign.

readLink.label: Read: The law of variable proportions, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: MP above AP → AP rising; MP below AP → AP falling

questions.stem: Total product is 70 units with 7 workers and remains 70 units with 8 workers. The marginal product of the 8th worker is:

options.text: 70 units
options.explanation: 70 is the total product, not the marginal product of the 8th worker.

options.text: 8.75 units
options.explanation: 8.75 is the average product with 8 workers (70 ÷ 8), not the marginal product.

options.text: 0 units
options.explanation: Correct. MP of the 8th worker = 70 − 70 = 0. Total product is at its maximum exactly when marginal product is zero.

options.text: 4 units
options.explanation: 4 is the marginal product of the 7th worker, not the 8th; the 8th adds nothing.

readLink.label: Read: The law of variable proportions, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: TP is maximum where MP = 0

questions.stem: A rational producer will always operate in which stage of the law of variable proportions?

options.text: Stage I
options.explanation: In Stage I the fixed factor is under-used and average product is still rising; a producer can gain by employing more of the variable factor, so it is not the stopping stage.

options.text: Stage II
options.explanation: Correct. Stage II — from the maximum of average product to where marginal product reaches zero — is the rational stage; the exact point within it depends on factor prices.

options.text: Stage III
options.explanation: In Stage III marginal product is negative and total product falls, so adding the variable factor reduces output — an irrational choice.

options.text: The producer is indifferent between all three stages
options.explanation: The producer is not indifferent; Stages I and III are both inefficient, leaving Stage II as the rational choice.

readLink.label: Read: The three stages of production, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: Rational producer operates in Stage II

questions.stem: In Stage III of the law of variable proportions:

options.text: total product rises at an increasing rate
options.explanation: That describes the early part of Stage I, not Stage III.

options.text: average product is at its maximum
options.explanation: Average product peaks at the end of Stage I / start of Stage II, not in Stage III.

options.text: marginal product is negative and total product falls
options.explanation: Correct. Stage III is the stage of negative returns: marginal product is below zero, so total product actually declines as more of the variable factor is added.

options.text: marginal product equals average product
options.explanation: MP equals AP at the boundary between Stage I and Stage II, not in Stage III.

readLink.label: Read: The three stages of production, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: Stage III: MP negative, TP falling

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Production · Variable proportions vs scale
questions.stem: Diminishing marginal returns under the law of variable proportions arise because:

options.text: all factors are increased together in the same proportion
options.explanation: That is the setting for returns to scale, not the law of variable proportions.

options.text: more of a variable factor is applied to a fixed factor, so the proportion between them changes
options.explanation: Correct. With one factor fixed, each extra unit of the variable factor has less of the fixed factor to work with, so beyond a point marginal product falls.

options.text: the prices of inputs rise as output increases
options.explanation: Diminishing returns is a physical (technical) relationship, not a result of rising input prices.

options.text: technology deteriorates as output rises
options.explanation: Technology is held constant; diminishing returns comes from the changing factor proportions, not from worsening technology.

readLink.label: Read: The law of variable proportions, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: Diminishing returns from adding a variable factor to a fixed factor (short run)

questions.stem: Returns to scale describe what happens to output when:

options.text: one variable factor is increased and the rest are held fixed
options.explanation: That is the short-run law of variable proportions, not returns to scale.

options.text: all factors are increased together in the same proportion, in the long run
options.explanation: Correct. Returns to scale is a long-run idea: every factor is increased in the same proportion and we ask how output responds.

options.text: the price of the output changes
options.explanation: Returns to scale concerns physical inputs and output, not the output price.

options.text: only the fixed factor is increased
options.explanation: Returns to scale increases all factors together; there is no fixed factor in the long run.

questions.sourceRef: Returns to scale: all factors increased in the same proportion (long run)

questions.stem: Increasing returns to scale means that when all inputs are increased in a given proportion, output increases:

options.text: in exactly the same proportion
options.explanation: Output rising in exactly the same proportion is constant returns to scale, not increasing.

options.text: in a smaller proportion
options.explanation: Output rising by a smaller proportion is decreasing returns to scale, not increasing.

options.text: in a greater proportion
options.explanation: Correct. Under increasing returns to scale output rises more than in proportion to the inputs — double the inputs and output more than doubles.

options.text: not at all
options.explanation: Output not changing is neither of the three returns-to-scale cases; increasing returns means a more-than-proportionate rise.

questions.sourceRef: Increasing returns to scale: output up more than in proportion to inputs

questions.stem: A firm doubles all of its inputs and finds that output rises from 500 units to 900 units. This is an example of:

options.text: increasing returns to scale
options.explanation: Increasing returns would need output to more than double (above 1,000). Here output less than doubled.

options.text: constant returns to scale
options.explanation: Constant returns would need output to exactly double to 1,000. Here it reached only 900.

options.text: decreasing returns to scale
options.explanation: Correct. Inputs doubled (a factor of 2) but output rose only from 500 to 900 — a factor of 1.8, less than 2 — so output rose less than in proportion: decreasing returns to scale.

options.text: negative returns to scale
options.explanation: Output rose, not fell, so returns are not negative; because the rise was less than proportionate, the case is decreasing returns to scale.

questions.sourceRef: Output factor 900/500 = 1.8 < input factor 2 → decreasing returns to scale

questions.stem: An isoquant is a curve that shows:

options.text: all combinations of two factors that yield the same level of output
options.explanation: Correct. An isoquant (equal-product curve) joins the input combinations that produce one and the same output — the producer's counterpart of the indifference curve.

options.text: all combinations of two factors that cost the same amount
options.explanation: Equal-cost combinations lie on the iso-cost line, not the isoquant.

options.text: all combinations of two goods that give the buyer equal satisfaction
options.explanation: Equal-satisfaction combinations lie on an indifference curve, a consumer concept, not an isoquant.

options.text: the total output at each level of a single input
options.explanation: That describes the total-product curve, not an isoquant, which involves two variable inputs.

readLink.label: Read: Isoquants and the iso-cost line, §5 →

questions.sourceRef: Isoquant = combinations of two factors giving equal output

questions.stem: An isoquant is convex to the origin because:

options.text: the marginal rate of technical substitution diminishes as more of one factor is used
options.explanation: Correct. As labour replaces capital along the isoquant, each extra unit of labour substitutes for less and less capital, so the MRTS falls and the curve is convex.

options.text: the marginal rate of technical substitution rises as more of one factor is used
options.explanation: A rising MRTS would make the curve concave, not convex. The MRTS diminishes.

options.text: the two factors are perfect substitutes
options.explanation: Perfect substitutes give a straight-line isoquant, not a convex one.

options.text: output rises as you move along the curve
options.explanation: Output is constant along one isoquant; convexity comes from the diminishing MRTS, not from a change in output.

readLink.label: Read: Isoquants and the iso-cost line, §5 →

questions.sourceRef: Isoquants convex owing to diminishing marginal rate of technical substitution

questions.stem: The slope of the iso-cost line is equal to:

options.text: the ratio of the marginal products of the two factors
options.explanation: The ratio of marginal products is the slope of the isoquant (the MRTS), not of the iso-cost line.

options.text: the ratio of the prices of the two factors
options.explanation: Correct. The iso-cost line shows the combinations affordable for a given outlay, and its slope is the ratio of the factor prices (wage of labour ÷ price of capital).

options.text: the level of output produced
options.explanation: Output is a feature of the isoquant, not the slope of the iso-cost line.

options.text: the total cost of production
options.explanation: Total cost fixes the position of the iso-cost line, not its slope; the slope is the price ratio.

readLink.label: Read: Isoquants and the iso-cost line, §5 →

questions.sourceRef: Slope of iso-cost line = ratio of factor prices (w ÷ r)

questions.stem: The wage rate of labour is ₹ 200 per unit and the price of capital is ₹ 100 per unit. At the least-cost combination, the marginal rate of technical substitution of labour for capital must equal:

options.explanation: 0.5 is the price of capital divided by the wage (100 ÷ 200); the MRTS of labour for capital equals the wage divided by the price of capital, which is the other way up.
Correct. At the least-cost combination MRTS of labour for capital = w ÷ r = 200 ÷ 100 = 2.
100 is the price of capital, not the ratio of the two factor prices.
300 is the sum of the two prices, which has no role in the equilibrium condition.

questions.sourceRef: At least-cost combination MRTS = w ÷ r = 200 ÷ 100 = 2

questions.stem: A producer minimising the cost of a given output is in equilibrium at the point where:

options.text: the iso-cost line is tangent to the highest attainable isoquant
options.explanation: Correct. Least cost for a given output is reached where the iso-cost line just touches (is tangent to) the highest isoquant it can reach; there MRTS equals the factor-price ratio.

options.text: the iso-cost line cuts the isoquant at two points
options.explanation: Where the iso-cost line cuts an isoquant, a cheaper combination on the same isoquant still exists; equilibrium is at tangency, not intersection.

options.text: the marginal products of the two factors are equal
options.explanation: Equilibrium equalises the marginal product per rupee, not the marginal products themselves, unless the factor prices happen to be equal.

options.text: total cost is at its maximum
options.explanation: The producer minimises cost for the output, not maximises it; equilibrium is the least-cost tangency.

questions.sourceRef: Producer equilibrium at tangency of iso-cost line and highest isoquant

questions.stem: At a firm's current input mix, the marginal product per rupee spent on capital exceeds the marginal product per rupee spent on labour. To reach the least-cost combination the firm should:

options.text: use more capital and less labour
options.explanation: Correct. When a rupee spent on capital buys more output than a rupee spent on labour, shifting spending toward capital (and away from labour) raises output per rupee until the two ratios are equal.

options.text: use more labour and less capital
options.explanation: That would widen the gap, moving away from equilibrium; the firm should favour the factor with the higher marginal product per rupee, which is capital.

options.text: keep the mix unchanged, since it is already optimal
options.explanation: The mix is not optimal: the marginal products per rupee are unequal, so a reallocation can lower cost.

options.text: reduce the use of both factors equally
options.explanation: Cutting both equally does not correct the imbalance in marginal product per rupee; the firm must shift toward capital.

questions.sourceRef: Reallocate toward the factor with higher MP per rupee until MPL/w = MPK/r

questions.stem: The expansion path of a firm shows:

options.text: the least-cost factor combinations at successive levels of output, with factor prices unchanged
options.explanation: Correct. The expansion path joins the tangency (least-cost) points as output rises while factor prices stay constant — the route the firm follows as it grows.

options.text: the combinations of two goods a consumer buys as income rises
options.explanation: That is the consumer's income-consumption path, not the producer's expansion path.

options.text: the way output changes when only one factor is varied
options.explanation: Varying one factor traces the total-product curve; the expansion path varies scale along least-cost points.

options.text: the points where the iso-cost line cuts the isoquants
options.explanation: The expansion path joins the tangency points, not the intersection points.

questions.sourceRef: Expansion path joins least-cost points as output rises at constant factor prices

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of an internal economy of scale?

options.text: A pool of skilled labour developing in the locality as the industry grows
options.explanation: A local labour pool benefits all firms in the industry — that is an external economy, not internal.

options.text: A firm obtaining a bulk-purchase discount on its raw materials as it expands
options.explanation: Correct. Buying inputs in bulk at a discount is a marketing (commercial) economy that a firm gains from its own expansion — an internal economy of scale.

options.text: Specialised repair firms setting up near a growing industry
options.explanation: Ancillary firms serving the whole industry are an external economy, available to every firm.

options.text: Better roads built because the whole industry expanded
options.explanation: Shared infrastructure from the industry's growth is an external economy, not an internal one.

questions.sourceRef: Internal economies arise from the firm's own expansion (e.g. bulk-buying discount)

questions.stem: External economies of scale are benefits that arise from:

options.text: the growth of a single firm alone
options.explanation: Benefits from one firm's own growth are internal economies, not external.

options.text: the growth of the whole industry, shared by all firms in it
options.explanation: Correct. External economies come from the expansion of the entire industry — a skilled-labour pool, ancillary firms, shared infrastructure — and every firm in the industry enjoys them.

options.text: a firm installing a larger, more efficient machine
options.explanation: A firm's own larger machine is a technical (internal) economy, not external.

options.text: a firm borrowing on better terms because it is large
options.explanation: Better borrowing terms from a firm's own size is a financial (internal) economy, not external.

questions.sourceRef: External economies arise from the growth of the whole industry

questions.stem: The most common cause of internal diseconomies of scale as a firm grows very large is:

options.text: difficulties of management, control and coordination
options.explanation: Correct. Beyond a point a firm becomes too big to manage well — decisions slow, supervision falters, coordination weakens — so cost per unit rises. Managerial diseconomy is the classic internal diseconomy.

options.text: a fall in the market price of the product
options.explanation: A falling product price affects revenue, not the firm's internal cost structure; it is not a diseconomy of scale.

options.text: rising local input prices as the whole industry expands
options.explanation: Rising local input prices from industry-wide growth are an external, not internal, diseconomy.

options.text: a bulk-purchase discount on raw materials
options.explanation: A bulk-purchase discount is an economy, not a diseconomy.

questions.sourceRef: Internal diseconomies are chiefly managerial (control and coordination)

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Cost · Accounting vs economic cost
questions.stem: Economic cost differs from accounting cost in that economic cost also includes:

options.text: only the explicit cash payments to outsiders
options.explanation: Explicit cash payments are exactly what accounting cost already records; economic cost adds something more.

options.text: the implicit costs of the firm's own factors
options.explanation: Correct. Economic cost = explicit (accounting) cost + implicit cost — the opportunity cost of the firm's own resources, which the books do not record.

options.text: the firm's total revenue
options.explanation: Revenue is not a cost; economic cost adds implicit costs, not receipts.

options.text: the taxes paid to the government
options.explanation: Taxes are explicit payments already in the accounting cost; the distinctive addition in economic cost is the implicit cost.

questions.sourceRef: Economic cost = explicit cost + implicit cost

questions.stem: Which of the following is an implicit cost?

options.text: Wages paid to hired workers
options.explanation: Wages to hired workers are an actual cash payment to outsiders — an explicit cost.

options.text: Rent paid for a hired factory building
options.explanation: Rent paid to a landlord is an explicit cash payment, not an implicit cost.

options.text: The salary the owner could have earned by working elsewhere
options.explanation: Correct. The owner's forgone salary is a cost of the firm's own factor for which no payment is made — an implicit cost, counted in economic but not accounting cost.

options.text: The price paid for raw materials
options.explanation: Raw-material purchases are explicit cash payments to suppliers, not implicit costs.

questions.sourceRef: Implicit cost = cost of the firm's own factors (e.g. owner's forgone salary)

questions.stem: The opportunity cost of using a resource in a particular way is:

options.text: the money originally paid to acquire the resource
options.explanation: The original outlay is the historical cost; opportunity cost is about the alternative use forgone, not the money spent.

options.text: the value of the next-best alternative that has to be given up
options.explanation: Correct. Opportunity cost is the benefit of the best alternative forgone — the true economic cost of any choice.

options.text: the total cost of all alternatives added together
options.explanation: Opportunity cost is the single next-best alternative forgone, not the sum of all alternatives.

options.text: zero, if the resource is already owned by the firm
options.explanation: An owned resource still has an opportunity cost — its best alternative use — which is exactly why implicit costs exist.

questions.sourceRef: Opportunity cost = value of the next-best alternative forgone

questions.stem: A sunk cost is one that:

options.text: has already been incurred and cannot be recovered, and so is irrelevant to a present decision
options.explanation: Correct. A sunk cost — past spending that cannot be got back — should be ignored when deciding what to do now, because no current choice can change it.

options.text: varies directly with the level of output
options.explanation: A cost that varies with output is a variable cost, not a sunk cost.

options.text: will be incurred only if the firm expands
options.explanation: A cost that depends on a future choice is not sunk; a sunk cost has already been incurred.

options.text: can always be fully recovered by resale
options.explanation: A fully recoverable cost is not sunk; the defining feature of a sunk cost is that it cannot be recovered.

questions.sourceRef: Sunk cost = already incurred, unrecoverable, irrelevant to present decisions

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Cost · Economic vs accounting profit
questions.stem: Because economic cost includes implicit costs that accounting cost ignores, a firm's economic profit is generally:

options.text: larger than its accounting profit
options.explanation: Adding implicit costs raises total cost, so economic profit is smaller, not larger, than accounting profit.

options.text: equal to its accounting profit
options.explanation: The two are equal only when implicit costs are zero; in general implicit costs are positive, so they differ.

options.text: smaller than its accounting profit
options.explanation: Correct. Economic cost = accounting cost + implicit cost, so economic profit = accounting profit − implicit cost, which is smaller.

options.text: always negative
options.explanation: Economic profit can be positive, zero or negative; it is simply smaller than accounting profit, not necessarily below zero.

questions.sourceRef: Economic profit = accounting profit − implicit cost, so it is smaller

questions.stem: A shopkeeper pays ₹ 8,000 in wages, ₹ 5,000 in rent and ₹ 12,000 for materials. He also forgoes a salary of ₹ 15,000 he could earn elsewhere and ₹ 3,000 of interest on his own capital. His total economic cost is:

options.explanation: ₹ 25,000 is only the explicit cost (8,000 + 5,000 + 12,000); economic cost must add the implicit costs too.
₹ 18,000 is only the implicit cost (15,000 + 3,000); economic cost includes the explicit cost as well.
₹ 40,000 omits the ₹ 3,000 forgone interest; the full implicit cost is ₹ 18,000, giving ₹ 43,000.

questions.sourceRef: Economic cost = explicit (25,000) + implicit (18,000) = 43,000

questions.stem: Which statement about total fixed cost (TFC) in the short run is correct?

options.text: It rises as output rises
options.explanation: That describes total variable cost. Total fixed cost does not change with output.

options.text: It is zero when output is zero
options.explanation: Total variable cost is zero at zero output; total fixed cost is positive even at zero output (rent, insurance).

options.text: It does not change with the level of output and is positive even at zero output
options.explanation: Correct. Fixed cost is the cost of the fixed factors; it stays the same at every output and must be paid even when nothing is produced.

options.text: It equals marginal cost at every output
options.explanation: Fixed cost is unrelated to marginal cost; indeed fixed cost does not enter marginal cost at all.

questions.sourceRef: TFC constant with output and positive at zero output

questions.stem: At an output of zero, total variable cost (TVC) is:

options.text: equal to total fixed cost
options.explanation: At zero output total cost equals total fixed cost, but total variable cost itself is zero.

options.text: zero
options.explanation: Correct. Variable cost is the cost of the variable factors, which are not used when nothing is produced, so TVC is zero at zero output.

options.text: at its maximum
options.explanation: Variable cost rises with output, so it is least (zero) at zero output, not greatest.

options.text: equal to total cost
options.explanation: At zero output total cost equals fixed cost, which is positive, while variable cost is zero; they are not equal here.

questions.sourceRef: TVC is zero at zero output

questions.stem: A firm's total fixed cost is ₹ 100 and its total variable cost at 5 units of output is ₹ 150. Its total cost at 5 units is:

options.explanation: ₹ 100 is the fixed cost alone; total cost also includes the variable cost.
₹ 150 is the variable cost alone; total cost adds the fixed cost.
Correct. TC = TFC + TVC = 100 + 150 = ₹ 250.
₹ 50 is the difference of the two figures, not their sum; total cost is TFC + TVC = ₹ 250.

questions.stem: Total fixed cost is ₹ 100. The average fixed cost at an output of 4 units is:

options.explanation: Correct. AFC = TFC ÷ Q = 100 ÷ 4 = ₹ 25.
₹ 30 is the average variable cost at 4 units in the schedule, not the average fixed cost.
₹ 55 is the average total cost at 4 units (AFC + AVC), not the average fixed cost alone.
₹ 20 would be 100 ÷ 5; at 4 units the average fixed cost is 100 ÷ 4 = ₹ 25.

questions.stem: Total variable cost is ₹ 120 at an output of 4 units. The average variable cost is:

options.explanation: ₹ 25 is the average fixed cost at 4 units (100 ÷ 4), not the average variable cost.
Correct. AVC = TVC ÷ Q = 120 ÷ 4 = ₹ 30.
₹ 55 is the average total cost at 4 units, not the average variable cost.
₹ 40 would be 120 ÷ 3; at 4 units the average variable cost is 120 ÷ 4 = ₹ 30.

questions.stem: Total cost is ₹ 220 at 4 units of output and ₹ 250 at 5 units. The marginal cost of the 5th unit is:

options.explanation: ₹ 50 is the average total cost at 5 units (250 ÷ 5), not the marginal cost.
Correct. MC = ΔTC = TC(5) − TC(4) = 250 − 220 = ₹ 30.
₹ 250 is the total cost at 5 units, not the marginal cost of the 5th unit.
₹ 20 is the marginal cost of an earlier unit in the schedule; the 5th unit's MC is 250 − 220 = ₹ 30.

questions.stem: Total cost is ₹ 300 at 6 units of output and ₹ 380 at 7 units. The marginal cost of the 7th unit is:

options.explanation: Correct. MC = ΔTC = TC(7) − TC(6) = 380 − 300 = ₹ 80.
₹ 50 is the marginal cost of the 6th unit in the schedule, not the 7th.
₹ 380 is the total cost at 7 units, not the marginal cost of the 7th unit.
₹ 54.29 is the average total cost at 7 units (380 ÷ 7), not the marginal cost.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Cost · Average fixed cost shape
questions.stem: As output rises, the average fixed cost curve:

options.text: falls continuously, approaching but never touching the horizontal axis
options.explanation: Correct. A fixed sum spread over more and more units gives an ever-smaller AFC; the curve is a rectangular hyperbola that keeps falling toward, but never reaches, zero.

options.text: is U-shaped
options.explanation: AVC, ATC and MC are U-shaped; AFC falls continuously and is not U-shaped.

options.text: rises continuously
options.explanation: AFC falls as output rises, because the fixed cost is divided among more units, not fewer.

options.text: stays constant at all outputs
options.explanation: Total fixed cost is constant, but average fixed cost per unit falls as output rises.

questions.sourceRef: AFC falls continuously (rectangular hyperbola)

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Cost · MC and AC relationship
questions.stem: The marginal cost curve cuts the average total cost curve at:

options.text: the minimum point of the average total cost curve
options.explanation: Correct. MC equals ATC at the lowest point of ATC; to the left MC is below ATC (ATC falling) and to the right MC is above ATC (ATC rising).

options.text: the maximum point of the average total cost curve
options.explanation: The ATC curve has no maximum in the relevant range; MC cuts it at its minimum, not a maximum.

options.text: a point where average total cost is rising
options.explanation: Where ATC is rising, MC lies above ATC and does not cross it; the crossing is at the ATC minimum.

options.text: the point where average fixed cost is zero
options.explanation: Average fixed cost never reaches zero, and the MC–ATC crossing is set by the ATC minimum, not by AFC.

questions.sourceRef: MC cuts ATC at the minimum of ATC

questions.stem: In a cost schedule, total cost is ₹ 250 at 5 units and ₹ 300 at 6 units. The average total cost at 5 units, and the marginal cost of the 6th unit, are respectively:

options.explanation: ₹ 62.50 is not 250 ÷ 5; the average total cost at 5 units is 250 ÷ 5 = ₹ 50.
Correct. ATC at 5 units = 250 ÷ 5 = ₹ 50; MC of the 6th unit = 300 − 250 = ₹ 50. MC equals ATC here, which is exactly the ATC minimum.
₹ 30 is not the average total cost at 5 units; 250 ÷ 5 = ₹ 50. The marginal cost figure is right.
₹ 55 is the ATC at 4 units and ₹ 80 the MC of the 7th unit; neither matches the 5-unit ATC (₹ 50) or the 6th-unit MC (₹ 50).

questions.sourceRef: ATC(5) = 250 ÷ 5 = 50; MC(6) = 300 − 250 = 50; MC = ATC at the ATC minimum

questions.topic: Ch 3 · Cost · MC and AC relationship
questions.stem: If marginal cost is below average cost at a given output, then average cost at that output must be:

options.text: rising
options.explanation: Average cost rises only when marginal cost is above it, not below it.

options.text: falling
options.explanation: Correct. When the marginal unit costs less than the running average, it pulls the average down, so average cost is falling.

options.text: at its minimum
options.explanation: Average cost is at its minimum only when marginal cost equals it, not when marginal cost is below it.

options.text: at its maximum
options.explanation: There is no maximum of the U-shaped average cost curve in this range; MC below AC means AC is falling.

questions.sourceRef: MC below AC → AC falling

questions.stem: An imperfectly competitive firm sells 2 units at a price of ₹ 18 each and 3 units at a price of ₹ 16 each. The marginal revenue of the 3rd unit is:

options.explanation: ₹ 16 is the price (average revenue) of the 3rd unit, not its marginal revenue. Under imperfect competition MR is below AR.
Correct. TR at 2 units = 18 × 2 = ₹ 36; TR at 3 units = 16 × 3 = ₹ 48; MR of the 3rd unit = 48 − 36 = ₹ 12.
₹ 48 is the total revenue at 3 units, not the marginal revenue of the 3rd unit.
₹ 2 is the fall in price from ₹ 18 to ₹ 16, not the marginal revenue, which is the change in total revenue (₹ 12).

questions.stem: The average revenue curve of a firm is the same as its:

options.text: demand curve
options.explanation: Correct. Average revenue equals price (AR = TR ÷ Q = price), so the AR curve plotted against quantity is exactly the firm's demand curve.

options.text: marginal cost curve
options.explanation: The AR curve is a revenue curve, unrelated to the marginal cost curve.

options.text: total cost curve
options.explanation: Total cost is a cost concept; the AR curve is revenue per unit, which equals the demand curve.

options.text: supply curve
options.explanation: The AR curve is the demand curve the firm faces, not the supply curve.

questions.sourceRef: AR = price, so the AR curve is the firm's demand curve

questions.stem: A firm under perfect competition sells its output at a fixed market price of ₹ 20 per unit, whatever the quantity. The marginal revenue from selling one more unit is:

options.explanation: Correct. When the price is constant, each extra unit adds exactly the price to total revenue, so MR = ₹ 20 = AR = price. Under perfect competition AR = MR.
₹ 80 would be the total revenue from 4 units, not the marginal revenue of one more unit.
₹ 5 does not follow from a constant price; the marginal revenue equals the price of ₹ 20.
Marginal revenue is zero only if selling more added nothing; at a constant price of ₹ 20 each extra unit adds ₹ 20.

questions.sourceRef: Perfect competition: price constant → MR = AR = price = 20
